title: A Milky Way for dinner?
caption: Yepun and the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Yepun, the fourth Unit Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile, seems to take a bite out of the colourful band of the Milky Way in this photograph. So what is our galaxy made of?

Mostly stars, planets, and plenty of gas and dust, all bound by gravity, plus a generous helping of dark matter. The Milky Way is a medium-sized disc with spiral arms, wrapped in an outer halo. The Solar System sits in one of the arms, some 25 000 light-years from the centre, so we see only part of the galaxy. Its core hides behind thick dust, concealing the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*, first imaged in 2022.

Astronomers estimate the galaxy holds between 100 and 400 billion stars, and probably as many planets. Older stars dominate the inner regions, while the arms are packed with young stars born from giant clouds of gas and dust. Out in the halo are globular clusters of old stars and the remains of small galaxies the Milky Way has swallowed.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph at Paranal; the source gives no camera or exposure details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure brings out the Milky Way's colours and dust lanes much more strongly than the eye would see them.

explore: Galaxies spin so fast that stars, gas and dust alone could not hold them together. Scientists think the Milky Way sits inside a vast halo of dark matter, probably ten times the mass of all its stars or more. Telescopes like the VLT help by probing how it affects visible matter.
alt: The VLT's Yepun telescope silhouetted against the colourful band of the Milky Way.
